note: Coconut reasons in hidden state rather than words, which removes the readable trace auditors currently rely on.
title: Training Large Language Models to Reason in a Continuous Latent Space
explain_beginner: When a chatbot solves a math or logic problem step by step, it usually writes out its reasoning in plain sentences before giving an answer, a habit called chain of thought. This paper asks whether a model could reason in a different way entirely, using its own internal numerical representations instead of words, and whether that could work better for problems that require exploring several possible paths before finding the right one. The authors built a system called Coconut that feeds a model's internal state back into itself as the next reasoning step, rather than translating that state into a sentence first. On logic puzzles that need real planning and backtracking, this approach reached higher accuracy than writing out reasoning in words, and it did so using far fewer computational steps. On grade school math problems the internal approach did not beat writing things out in words, so the benefit was not universal. The tradeoff is that this internal reasoning is invisible to a human reader, since there is no readable sentence to check.
explain_business: This is early stage research, not a deployable feature, and no current commercial model uses this technique. But it points to a real tension worth tracking. A common way businesses gain confidence in an AI system's answer is by reading the step by step reasoning it produces along the way, and using that trail for auditing, debugging, or compliance review. This paper shows that reasoning does not have to be produced as readable text to work, and in some cases works better and faster when it is not. If latent reasoning like this eventually reaches production systems, it would improve speed and possibly accuracy on planning heavy tasks, but it would also remove the readable trace that today lets a human or an automated checker verify how an answer was reached. Anyone building governance or audit processes around chain of thought output should treat that visibility as a current convenience rather than a permanent guarantee, since the field is actively exploring reasoning methods that do not produce it at all.
explain_practitioner: Coconut replaces explicit chain of thought tokens with the model's last hidden state, fed back in as the next input embedding, so reasoning happens in continuous latent space rather than in language. Training uses a multi stage curriculum that starts from ordinary text based chain of thought and gradually swaps early reasoning steps for blocks of continuous thoughts, with the optimizer reset at each stage. The authors evaluate on GSM8k for arithmetic word problems, ProntoQA for simple multi hop logical inference, and a new benchmark they built called ProsQA, which uses graphs of logical relationships with distractor branches to force genuine search rather than pattern matching. On the harder planning heavy tasks, ProntoQA and ProsQA, Coconut matched or beat standard chain of thought while producing far shorter outputs. On GSM8k it underperformed chain of thought on raw accuracy. The authors are explicit that the curriculum is not optional. A version trained without it performed no better than skipping reasoning entirely, and scaling to a larger Llama 3 model produced smaller gains than on the smaller GPT-2 base.
